Even if one day time blows out all the lamps of my memories,  
If my own name starts to feel like a stranger to me,  
If a mirror shows me my face but cannot tell me my story,  
And I become a traveler on the paths of my own life,  
Even then I believe that love finds its own way.

If I lose my memory,  
And one day I walk past you, unaware,  
Maybe I won’t recognize you,  
Your voice won’t be able to open the door to my past,  
And your smile, like a forgotten photograph,  
Will only pause in my heart for a moment.

But then something strange will happen.  
My heart, which can no longer read the book of memories,  
Will surely recognize your presence.  
In the light of your eyes I will find peace,  
In your silence I will hear a familiar tune,  
And coming close to you will feel  
Like a bird that has wandered for centuries  
Finally reaching its nest.

I may not know your name,  
But I will smile at you without meaning to.  
I may not be able to say  
How many dreams we saw together,  
But the desire to dream new dreams  
Will still be born in my heart.

Because true love  
Does not depend on memory.  
It is written on the pages of the soul,  
Where even the dust of time cannot leave its mark.  
It lives in the beats of the heart,  
Where even forgetting cannot erase it.

So even if one day I forget everything,  
My past, my identity, my story,  
And one day walk past you in silence,  
I am certain  
My heart will choose you again.  
I will fall in love with you again,  
As if it were the first time,  
But this time just as true,  
Just as selfless,  
And maybe even deeper than before.

Because some loves are not written by memory,  
They are written by fate;  
And fate always  
Leads love back to its true address.

7/4/26, 6:12 PM - Johnny TEC. Dev: I don't hate animal
7/4/26, 6:12 PM - Johnny TEC. Dev: 👀
7/4/26, 6:13 PM - 𓃵 𝑴𝒆𝒔𝒔𝒊 | The GOAT ⚽ 𓃵 𝑴𝒆𝒔𝒔𝒊 | The GOAT ⚽: *1. What the Qur'an actually says about dogs* 
The Qur'an mentions dogs 3 times, and never with hate.  
- In *Surah Al-Kahf 18:18, 22* the dog of the People of the Cave is mentioned with respect. It guarded them and is described as stretching its paws at the entrance.  
- In *Surah Al-Ma'idah 5:4* Allah says you can eat what trained hunting dogs catch for you. So dogs used for work were considered useful.


*2. Then where does "haram/impure" come from?*  
That comes mainly from Hadith about cleanliness and Angels not entering a house with a dog, and about wudu if a dog licks something. Some scholars use that to say dogs are _najis_/impure for ritual purposes, not that the animal itself is evil.  
Also, dogs were used as guard dogs, hunting dogs, and herding dogs by the Prophet ﷺ and the Sahaba.

*3. Kindness to dogs in Islam*  
Islam commands kindness to _all_ living creatures. There are clear examples:
- A man was forgiven all his sins because he gave water to a thirsty dog. *Bukhari, Muslim*
- A woman was punished because she locked up a cat and didn’t feed it. *Bukhari, Muslim*  
The principle is: "There is reward in being kind to every living being."

So even scholars who say dogs are impure for prayer still say: don't abuse them, don't hate them, don't kill them without reason. Feed them, give them water, treat them well.

*In short:*  
Dogs are not mentioned in the Qur'an as something to hate. Some rulings about ritual purity exist, but mercy is the bigger rule in Islam. The Prophet ﷺ taught us: _“The merciful are shown mercy by the Most Merciful.”_

Allah cares about how we treat His creature

7/5/26, 12:01 PM - 𓃵 𝑴𝒆𝒔𝒔𝒊 | The GOAT ⚽ 𓃵 𝑴𝒆𝒔𝒔𝒊 | The GOAT ⚽: In Islamic jurisprudence, the topic of music and musical instruments is a subject of detailed discussion among scholars. Based on the Quran, Hadith, and the consensus of the majority of classical scholars (including the four main schools of thought), your statement reflects the mainstream, traditional Islamic position.
Here is a breakdown of the Islamic perspective on music and the specific allowance of the Daff (tambourine/frame drum), supported by textual evidence.
1. The Prohibition of General Music and Instruments
The majority of Islamic scholars hold that conventional musical instruments (like string, wind, and modern electronic instruments) and singing that promotes vain desires are forbidden (Haram).
Evidence from the Quran
The primary verse cited by scholars regarding the prohibition of music is found in Surah Luqman:
"And of mankind is he who purchases idle talks (lahwal-hadith) to mislead (men) from the path of Allah without knowledge, and takes it (the path of Allah) by way of mockery. For such there will be a humiliating torment."
— Surah Luqman (31:6)
Scholar Commentary: When the prominent companion Abdullah ibn Mas’ud (R.A.) was asked about the phrase "idle talks" (lahwal-hadith), he swore by Allah three times that it referred to music and singing. Other major companions like Ibn Abbas (R.A.) and Jabir (R.A.) held the same view.
Evidence from the Hadith
The most explicit prohibition of musical instruments comes from a well-known narration in Sahih al-Bukhari:
The Prophet (\rho) said: "There will be among my Ummah people who will regard as permissible adultery, silk, alcohol, and musical instruments (al-ma'azif)..."
— Sahih al-Bukhari (5590)
Scholarly Insight: The Arabic word al-ma'azif refers strictly to stringed instruments and musical equipment in general. Because the Prophet (\rho) grouped musical instruments together with major sins like adultery and alcohol, scholars deduce that they are inherently forbidden.
2. The Exception: The Playing of the Daff
While general musical instruments are prohibited, Islamic law makes a specific exception for the Daff.
A Daff is a traditional, single-headed frame drum (similar to a tambourine but strictly without the metal jingles or cymbals). It is played by hand, not with sticks like a Dhol or modern snare drum.
The Prophet (\rho) permitted, and sometimes encouraged, the beating of the Daff to announce joyful Islamic occasions, primarily weddings (Nikah) and Eid celebrations.
Evidence from Hadith for the Daff
For Weddings:
The Prophet (\rho) said:
"The distinction between what is lawful (Halal) and what is unlawful (Haram) in marriage is the beating of the daff and the raising of voices (with innocent singing) for the wedding."
— Sunan an-Nasa'i (3369), graded Hasan
For Eid Celebrations:
Aisha (R.A.) narrated that on the day of Eid, two young girls were singing and beating the Daff in her house. When her father, Abu Bakr (R.A.), entered, he scolded them, saying, "The musical instrument of Shaytan in the house of the Messenger of Allah?"
The Prophet (\rho) turned to him and said: "O Abu Bakr, leave them alone, for every nation has its Eid, and today is our Eid."
— Sahih al-Bukhari (952)
Summary of Rules Regarding the Daff vs. Other Drums

7/20/26, 10:03 AM - 𓃵 𝑴𝒆𝒔𝒔𝒊 | The GOAT ⚽ 𓃵 𝑴𝒆𝒔𝒔𝒊 | The GOAT ⚽: Here is a breakdown and explanation of the phrase provided:
1. Line-by-Line Translation
「サナ、愛してるよ。」
English: "Sana, I love you."
Breakdown:
サナ (Sana): A personal name.
愛してるよ (Aishiteru yo): A direct, explicit declaration of romantic or deep love ("I love you"), with the emphasis particle yo.
「何を見せてほしいの、モトゥ。」
English: "What do you want me to show you, Motu?" / "What do you want to see, Motu?"
Breakdown:
何 (Nani): What.
見せてほしい (Misete hoshii): Expresses a desire for someone to show something ("I want [you] to show [me]").
の (no): A gentle sentence-ending particle used in questions.
モトゥ (Motu): A name or affectionate nickname (likely derived from a Hindi/Urdu term of endearment or personal name).
「サナ、愛してるよ。」
English: "Sana, I love you." (Repetition of the first line)
2. Context & Overall Meaning
Put together in natural English:
"Sana, I love you. What do you want me to show you, Motu? Sana, I love you."
Nuance & Tone
Affectionate & Intimate: The use of 愛してる (Aishiteru) is very strong and serious in Japanese—it is rarely used casually and carries deep emotional weight.
Multilingual Influence: The names/terms Sana and Motu (often a playful Hindi/Urdu term meaning "chubby" or used as a pet name) suggest this was likely translated into Japanese from another language (such as English, Hindi, or Urdu) or written by a non-native speaker expressing affection.
